name: Polymorphic Ventricular Tachycardia and Ventricular Fibrillation

clinicalPearls: Sustained polymorphic VT shows a QRS configuration that changes continuously beat to beat, reflecting an ever-changing ventricular activation sequence; unlike monomorphic VT it does not necessarily imply a fixed structural abnormality or single automatic focus (p.1968).
Sustained polymorphic VT commonly degenerates into ventricular fibrillation (p.1969).

Acute myocardial infarction or ischemia is a frequent cause and should be the first consideration; roughly 10% of acute MI patients develop VT that degenerates to VF, with greatest risk in the first hour (p.1969).
Polymorphic VT/VF occurring within the first 48 hours of acute MI carries higher in-hospital mortality, but survivors to discharge are not at increased risk of later arrhythmic sudden death (p.1969).

Torsades des pointes is the polymorphic VT linked to QT prolongation and classically begins in a pause-dependent fashion: a PVC induces a pause, the following sinus beat has a longer QT, and a PVC interrupting that T wave starts the run (p.1969).

Congenital long QT syndrome stems from ion-channel gene mutations; LQTS-1, -2, and -3 account for roughly 80-90% of cases, with LQTS-1/-2 involving potassium channels and LQTS-3 involving the sodium channel (p.1969-1970).

Genotype influences triggers: LQTS-1 events tend to occur during exertion (notably swimming), LQTS-2 with sudden auditory stimuli or emotional upset, and LQTS-3 sudden death tends to occur during sleep (p.1970).

Brugada syndrome causes syncope or cardiac arrest from polymorphic VT in the absence of structural heart disease; arrest may occur during sleep or be provoked by febrile illness, and males are more commonly affected (p.1970).

Catecholaminergic polymorphic VT is a rare familial disorder of abnormal sarcoplasmic calcium handling producing arrhythmias resembling digitalis toxicity, often with bidirectional (alternating QRS morphology) VT, presenting in childhood with exertion- or emotion-induced events (p.1971).
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, the most common genetic cardiovascular disorder (about 1 in 500), is a prominent cause of sudden death before age 35, typically via polymorphic VT/VF (p.1971).

Ventricular fibrillation shows disordered electrical ventricular activation with no identifiable QRS complexes; spiral wave reentry and multiple circulating reentry wavefronts are proposed mechanisms (p.1971).

After surviving acute MI and revascularization, poorly coupled but surviving Purkinje fibers (which tolerate ischemia owing to glycogen stores and oxygenation from the LV cavity) can trigger PVCs and ventricular fibrillation (p.1971).
harrison.pathophysiology: Polymorphic VT arises from a continually changing ventricular activation sequence. Proposed mechanisms include reentry with variable paths, spiral wave reentry, and multiple automatic foci, often near fibrotic myocardium and potentiated by damaged Purkinje cells or ventricular hypertrophy. Abnormal transmural dispersion of repolarization can drive it in the setting of channelopathies or antiarrhythmic drugs even without structural disease. In acute MI/ischemia, reentry through the infarct border zone is implicated, and surviving automatic Purkinje cells can initiate it. Torsades des pointes is associated with abnormal QT prolongation and pause-dependent initiation. Congenital LQTS reflects mutations in ion-channel genes governing repolarization (potassium channels in LQTS-1/-2, sodium channel in LQTS-3, and calcium channels in others). Short QT syndrome reflects a gain of function of the IKr potassium channel or reduced inward depolarizing currents. Brugada syndrome reflects dispersion of repolarization across the ventricular wall, with epicardial and M cells more affected than endocardial cells, localized to the right ventricular outflow tract; sodium channel mutations (SCN5A, SCN1B, SCN10A) are found in about 25% of cases. Catecholaminergic polymorphic VT results from cardiac ryanodine receptor (and less often calsequestrin 2) mutations causing abnormal sarcoplasmic calcium handling. Ventricular fibrillation represents disordered activation without organized QRS, frequently as degeneration of sustained polymorphic or monomorphic VT (p.1968-1971).
additionalDifferentials: Monomorphic ventricular tachycardia (implies a fixed structural substrate or automatic focus, unlike polymorphic VT)
Acquired (drug- or electrolyte-induced) long QT with torsades des pointes
Genetic dilated cardiomyopathies (e.g., Lamin A/C, SCN5A)
nonInfectiousMimics: Brugada pattern ST elevation must be distinguished from LV hypertrophy, pericarditis, myocardial ischemia/MI, hyperkalemia, hypothermia, right bundle branch block, and arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy (p.1970)
Asymptomatic Brugada ECG pattern versus the clinical Brugada syndrome (analogous to Wolff-Parkinson-White pattern versus syndrome)
J-point elevation as a benign normal variant versus early repolarization syndrome associated with arrhythmia risk
additionalInvestigations: 12-lead ECG with measurement of corrected QT (QTc); congenital LQTS typically prolongs QTc to >440 ms in men and >460 ms in women (p.1969)
Short QT syndrome: QTc <360 ms, usually <300 ms (p.1970)
Telemetry/rhythm strip to capture pause-dependent initiation of torsades and characteristic morphologies (p.1969)
Genetic testing/genotyping for family screening and diagnostic reassurance in LQTS (p.1970)
Provocative sodium channel blocker testing (e.g., flecainide, ajmaline, procainamide) to unmask Brugada ST elevation (p.1970)
Assessment of residual LV function/ejection fraction to guide ICD decisions (p.1969)
Reference resource crediblemeds.org to check whether a medication has been reported to prolong the QT interval (p.1969)
redFlags: Near-syncope, syncope, or cardiac arrest as the presenting event (p.1969)
Repeated episodes of polymorphic VT suggesting ongoing myocardial infarction/inadequate reperfusion (p.1969)
QTc exceeding 500 ms, female gender, and prior syncope or cardiac arrest as markers of increased risk in LQTS (p.1970)
Family history of sudden death (relevant in Brugada syndrome, early repolarization syndrome, and genetic cardiomyopathies) (p.1970-1971)
Febrile illness provoking cardiac arrest in Brugada syndrome (p.1970)
HCM features: young age, nonsustained VT, failure of blood pressure to rise with exercise, recent syncope (within 6 months), ventricular wall thickness >3 cm (p.1971)
harrison.prognosis: Polymorphic VT/VF within the first 48 hours of acute MI is associated with greater in-hospital mortality, yet patients who survive to discharge are not at increased risk for later arrhythmic sudden death. Long-term risk after infarction is governed largely by residual LV function. In LQTS, higher risk is conferred by QTc >500 ms, female gender, and prior syncope or cardiac arrest. HCM is a prominent cause of sudden death before age 35; surgical myectomy carries a sudden death rate <1% per year, and transcoronary ethanol septal ablation has a reported annual rate of sustained VT or sudden death of roughly 1-5% (p.1969-1971).
pitfalls: Assuming polymorphic VT implies a fixed structural focus as monomorphic VT does (p.1968)
Overlooking ongoing ischemia/inadequate reperfusion when polymorphic VT/VF recurs after MI (p.1969)
Failing to recognize numerous noncardiac QT-prolonging drugs and drug interactions that raise levels of an offending agent as precipitants of torsades (p.1969)
Re-exposing a patient who had QT-prolongation-induced polymorphic VT to QT-prolonging medications; such patients should be considered susceptible and avoid all future exposure (p.1969)
Misinterpreting benign J-point elevation (a common normal variant) as pathologic early repolarization syndrome (p.1971)
Confusing the asymptomatic Brugada ECG pattern with true Brugada syndrome (p.1970)
harrison.severityClassification: No single formal severity grade; risk is stratified by substrate. In post-MI patients, an ICD is indicated for persistent severe LV dysfunction (LV ejection fraction <35%). In LQTS, high-risk features include QTc >500 ms, female gender, and prior syncope/cardiac arrest. In HCM, high-risk markers include young age, nonsustained VT, failure of blood pressure to rise with exercise, recent syncope, and ventricular wall thickness >3 cm (p.1969-1971).
management: Immediate defibrillation for ventricular fibrillation or pulseless polymorphic VT with advanced life support
For torsades de pointes, intravenous magnesium, withdrawal of QT-prolonging drugs and correction of hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia, with overdrive pacing or isoprenaline for pause-dependent runs
Urgent reperfusion and revascularisation with beta-blockade when polymorphic VT complicates acute myocardial ischaemia or infarction
Long-term beta-blockade and strict avoidance of QT-prolonging drugs in congenital long QT syndrome
Implantable cardioverter-defibrillator for secondary prevention and for high arrhythmic risk, guided by residual left ventricular function
Disease-specific measures for other channelopathies, including quinidine and trigger avoidance in Brugada syndrome
Genetic testing with cascade family screening for inherited arrhythmia syndromes
Cardiology and electrophysiology referral for risk stratification and device or catheter ablation therapy
